newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Mossgas says it should be listed.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Mossgas says it should be listed.

text.p: State-owned oil from gas producer Mossgas said on Wednesday it would make a good candidate for a listing on the stock exchange despite the failed search last year for a buyer.

Chief executive Dave Day on Wednesday told the parliamentary minerals and energy committee that Mossgas, which owes 10.6 billion rand to the state and has limited gas reserves, would never be sold to one buyer in its present state.
"And that is precisely what happened when Mossgas was put up for sale last year, and there were no takers," Day said.

"Mossgas is worth a lot to the state but until such time as we know how much gas there is there, we have got this business of subsidies sorted out and Mossgas can earn commercial prices for its product, we are not going to be able to sell it.

"This is a company that you should float on the stock exchange and let the investment fraternity, the public and institutions, let them work out what the share price should be and let the market forces of supply and demand tell you what it is worth asa commercial enterprise."

He was reacting to criticism that Mossgas was a "white elephant" that the state should no longer support through subsidies and loans, and should not allow to invest any more funds in extending the life of its gas fields.
He was particularly critical of the fact that this kind of thinking had led to the decision to reduce the tariff protection provided to Mossgas.
Cabinet had decided in August 1993 that Mossgas should receive tariff protection for 10 years at $23 a barrel.
A report by Arthur Anderson business consultants recently said that Sasol Ltd should stop receiving tariff protection, it had not mentioned Mossgas at all.
But it had been assumed by the department that Mossgas would be affected by this decision as well.
"This is unfair and irregular and in fact we should be receiving $23 until the year 2003," Day said.
This would enable it to do its exploration work, invest in the chemicals side and be as profitable as previously state-owned and now listed Sasol Ltd had become.
Tariff protection had been introduced to provide a floor price to synthetic fuel producers.
Day said that Mossgas had been restricted to certain offshore leases but that more work was needed in surrounding areas to determine how much gas there actually was in the Bredasdorp Basin.
